note: Canto 21 ended with a shout from the souls of Saturn so loud that Dante could not make out a word of it. He turns to Beatrice stunned and frightened.

context: She comforts him as a mother comforts a frightened child, one of several moments in Paradiso where she is more mother than beloved.

quote: how the singing would have transformed you
note: The reason for Saturn's silence, given in Canto 21. If one shout shook him this much, the song of this heaven and Beatrice's smile would have destroyed him.

The souls were praying for God to punish the corrupt clergy that Peter Damian had just described. Beatrice promises Dante will see it in his lifetime. No one knows what event is meant. Some point to the humiliation of Pope Boniface VIII in 1303, others take it as a general promise.
God's justice comes at its own right moment. It only seems slow to those who long for it, and sudden to those who dread it.

context: He never gives his name. He identifies himself by the mountain where he built his monastery, and Dante's readers knew at once who was meant.

note: If Dante could see how much these souls love him, he would not be shy of asking. Benedict answers the question anyway, since he can read it in God.
Monte Cassino, a mountain between Rome and Naples. Around 529 Benedict founded on its summit the monastery that became the mother house of Western monks.

Pagans. According to the life of Benedict written by Pope Gregory the Great, the country people still worshipped at a temple of Apollo on the summit. Benedict broke the idol and built chapels in its place.
The souls of Saturn gave their lives to contemplation: prayer and thought fixed on God, away from the business of the world. Most were monks or hermits.

One of the first monks, a hermit of the Egyptian desert in the fourth century. Two saints of that name lived there at the same time, Macarius of Egypt and Macarius of Alexandria, and Dante may not have told them apart. He stands for the monks of the East.
Saint Romuald of Ravenna, who died in 1027. He founded the Camaldolese order, monks who lived as hermits, named for their house at Camaldoli in the mountains east of Florence.
Since the heaven of Mercury the souls have been hidden inside their own light. Dante asks to see Benedict's human face. It is the only time in Paradiso he makes this request.

context: There Dante will see the blessed in their human forms. Benedict is pointed out among them in Paradiso 32.

quote: it is not in space, nor turns on axes
note: The nine heavens below are physical spheres that spin around the earth. The Empyrean has no place and no motion. Nothing in it changes position, because nothing in it lacks anything it would need to move toward.

context: The golden stairway Dante saw in Canto 21. Benedict now says where it leads and why Dante could not see its top.
In Genesis 28 Jacob, asleep with a stone for a pillow, dreams of a ladder from earth to heaven with angels going up and down it.

note: The ladder is the life of contemplation, and Benedict's Rule itself describes a ladder of humility that monks climb to God. Now, he says, no monk even takes his feet off the ground.

The Rule of Saint Benedict, a short book that lays out the monk's day of prayer, reading and manual work. Nearly all monasteries in western Europe followed it. He says it is now only copied out, not kept.
The words of Jesus when he drove the merchants out of the Temple: "My house shall be called the house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves" (Matthew 21:13).
The hooded robes of monks. They are now sacks of spoiled flour: the habit is the same, but what is inside has gone bad.
Lending money at interest, which the medieval Church condemned as a grave sin. Dante punishes it in Inferno 17. Benedict says the greed of monks offends God even more.
The income from a monastery's lands. It is meant for the poor, and monks who have vowed poverty are taking it for themselves.
The Church's wealth is held in trust for the poor. Monks are spending it on their relatives, or, he hints, on mistresses and their children.

quote: from the oak's sprouting to its bearing acorns
note: An oak takes many years to bear its first acorns. Good beginnings among men go bad in less time than that.

context: "Silver and gold have I none", Peter says to a lame beggar at the Temple gate before healing him (Acts 3:6). The Church began with nothing.
Benedict names three founders, each of whom began in poverty: Peter the Church, himself the monks, Francis the friars.

note: Two miracles of the Old Testament: the Red Sea parted to let Israel escape from Egypt (Exodus 14), and the river Jordan stopped so that Israel could cross into the promised land (Joshua 3). Psalm 114 sings of both together.

Dante's Italian says it the other way round: the Jordan turned back and the sea in flight were greater wonders than rescue here would be. The usual reading is hopeful. God has done harder things than reform the monks, so help can still come.
Dante is still in his body, which by nature should fall, not rise. Beatrice sends him up the ladder with a gesture.
The last of the poem's direct addresses to the reader. It is an oath: as I hope to return one day to Heaven, what I say is true.
Gemini, the Twins, the next sign of the zodiac after Taurus. Dante enters the heaven of the stars at the very constellation he was born under.

Dante addresses the stars of Gemini. Astrologers held that this sign gave a gift for learning and writing. He credits the stars with his talent, though elsewhere he insists that they incline a person and do not compel.
The sun. It was in Gemini when Dante was born, which puts his birthday between the middle of May and the middle of June 1265. This is the only evidence for the date.

context: Dante was born in Florence, the chief city of Tuscany.

quote: the great wheel that turns you round
context: Dante stays in this heaven from here to Canto 27. In it he sees the triumph of Christ and is examined on faith, hope and love.

note: The hardest part of the poem, now beginning: to describe the highest heavens and at last the sight of God. Some take it as the examinations ahead, or as Dante's own death. He asks his birth stars for strength, as he has earlier asked the Muses and Apollo.

A look back through all seven planets to the earth. Dante has models: in Cicero's Dream of Scipio a Roman general is shown the tiny earth from the stars and learns to despise earthly fame, and Boethius repeats the lesson in the Consolation of Philosophy.
The earth, which Dante and his educated contemporaries knew to be a sphere. From the stars it looks so small and poor that he smiles.
The moon. Latona bore the twins Apollo and Diana, and Diana was goddess of the moon.
The dark patches on the moon. In Paradiso 2 Dante thought they came from thinner and denser matter, and Beatrice corrected him. From above he sees the moon's far side, which has no spots.
The sun. In Greek myth the Titan Hyperion was father of Helios, the sun god. Dante can now look straight at it.
The planets Mercury and Venus, named here by their mothers: Maia was the mother of Mercury, Dione of Venus. Both planets are always seen close to the sun.
Jupiter lies between Saturn, his father in myth, and Mars, his son. Astrologers held Saturn cold and Mars hot, with Jupiter temperate between them.

A famous image. A threshing floor is a small patch of beaten earth where grain is separated from the husk. Seen from the stars, the whole inhabited world is no bigger, and it is the thing men kill each other for.
Dante's Italian says from the hills to the river mouths: the whole of the inhabited land, from its heights down to its coasts.
The eyes of Beatrice. After a last look at the earth, Dante turns away from it for good.
